newsitem.title: SPAIN: Gonzalez safe from "dirty war" questioning for now.
newsitem.headline: Gonzalez safe from "dirty war" questioning for now.

text.p: Spanish Supreme Court judges voted six to four on Tuesday against questioning former prime minister Felipe Gonzalez about a 1980s "dirty war" on Basque separatists.

After six hours of closed-door debate in the top tribunal's second chamber, which deals with members of parliament like Gonzalez, Justice Jose Augusto de Vega told reporters six judges had voted against calling the Socialist leader. The other four cast dissenting votes.
The split decision let the former prime minister off the hook for now but state prosecutors warned they may reverse their advice not to call him if new evidence emerges.

Gonzalez, who lost elections in March after 13 years in power, denies charges by former security chiefs and disgruntled fellow Socialists that he knew of the 1983-87 campaign of bombings, kidnappings, torture and murders by members of the security forces and hired gunmen that killed 28 people.

Despite the "dirty war" scandal and a long string of Socialist corruption cases, he remains hugely popular and even has a tiny advantage in opinion polls now over Jose Maria Aznar, his conservative victor in the March elections.
Prosecutor Jose Maria Luzon's advice against questioning the former prime minister was important but not binding on the court -- and his boss said it may yet change if fresh proof surfaces.

"This decision has no bearing on others which, should there be new elements to take into account, could be taken while the investigation proceeds," Attorney-General Juan Ortiz Urculo said in a press statement after Luzon's court appearance on Monday.
Gonzalez himself was not in court on Monday but called a news conference about the refugee crisis in central Africa and refused to answer any questions about the top tribunal's impending ruling.
"How am I waiting for it? This is how I'm waiting," he shrugged when reporters asked him about the proceedings.

Technically, the 10 judges were deciding on an appeal about whether the Socialist leader should be questioned in the chief case in the covert campaign -- the mistaken-identity kidnapping in December 1983 of Basque businessman Segundo Marey.

One of the judges, investigating justice Eduardo Moner, had ruled in April that there was insufficient evidence to summon Gonzalez. The second chamber's ruling early on Tuesday was on an appeal against that decision lodged by relatives of the victims.
Also safe from questioning together with Gonzalez are his former minister Narcis Serra and Socialist leader Jose Maria Benegas, both of whom were included in Tuesday's decision.

The only new accusations against Gonzalez since Moner's April decision have come from Luis Roldan, a former Socialist head of the paramilitary Civil Guard who is himself accused of fraud and embezzlement while in office.
Roldan has testified that the operations against presumed rebels from ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) were official government policy and that Gonzalez was fully involved.

Gonzalez's first interior minister, Jose Barrionuevo, is already on trial at the Supreme Court on charges of masterminding and funding the shadowy death squads known as the GAL (the Spanish initials for Anti-terrorist Liberation Groups).
A senior Civil Guard general who commanded the force's main base in the Basque country is also on trial.

The new conservative government has accused Gonzalez of having waged "bodeguilla terrorism" -- a reference to a wine-cellar in his official residence where he entertained friends and hatched strategies with his closest aides.
